glossary.mmol/L: Millimoles per litre, the unit used for blood glucose concentration in the UK.
glossary.tremor: Involuntary shaking, here caused by adrenaline release.
glossary.palpitations: An unpleasant awareness of your own heartbeat, often fast or pounding.
glossary.drowsiness: Abnormal sleepiness, a sign that brain function is falling.
glossary.seizures: Bursts of abnormal electrical brain activity causing fits or altered awareness.
glossary.slurred speech: Unclear, poorly articulated speech from impaired brain function.
glossary.tachycardia: Heart rate above 100 beats per minute.
glossary.pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour: A tumour of hormone-producing pancreatic cells; an insulinoma is the commonest functional one.
glossary.functional tumour: A tumour that secretes an active hormone and causes symptoms from that hormone.
glossary.finger-prick: A bedside capillary blood glucose test using a drop of blood from the fingertip.
glossary.laboratory blood glucose: A venous blood sample sent to the lab to confirm the bedside glucose reading.
glossary.serum: The fluid part of blood left after clotting, used for many lab tests.
glossary.pre-proinsulin: The first precursor molecule made in beta cells, later trimmed to proinsulin and then insulin.
glossary.hormonal profile: A set of hormone levels (insulin, pro-insulin, C-peptide, ketones) taken at the moment of hypoglycaemia.
glossary.ketones: Acids made from fat breakdown; low during insulin-driven hypoglycaemia because insulin blocks their production.
glossary.oral fast-acting glucose: Quickly absorbed sugar by mouth, such as glucose tablets or a sugary drink.
glossary.glucose tablets: Chewable tablets of pure glucose used to treat a hypo quickly.
glossary.IV: Intravenous: given directly into a vein.
glossary.IV glucose: Glucose solution given into a vein, used when the patient cannot take sugar by mouth.
glossary.stat: Given immediately, as a single dose.
glossary.10% glucose: A glucose solution containing 10 g of glucose per 100 ml.
glossary.20% glucose: A more concentrated glucose solution, 20 g per 100 ml, so a smaller volume is needed.
glossary.longer-acting carbohydrate: Slowly absorbed starchy food such as toast or biscuits, given after a hypo to stop glucose falling again.
glossary.neonatal unit: The hospital ward that cares for sick or premature newborn babies.
glossary.neonates: Newborn babies in their first 28 days of life.
glossary.medication review: A structured check of all a patient's drugs and doses to find the cause of problems.
glossary.adrenaline: A stress hormone from the adrenal glands that raises glucose and triggers sweating, tremor and palpitations.
glossary.sympathetic: The fight-or-flight part of the autonomic nervous system.
glossary.neuropathy: Damage to nerves, causing loss of their normal function.
glossary.unheralded: Happening without any warning symptoms beforehand.
glossary.primary energy source: The main fuel a tissue uses; for the brain this is glucose.
glossary.mistimed: Given at the wrong time relative to food, so insulin peaks when there is no glucose coming in.
glossary.missed meals: Skipping food while on insulin or sulphonylureas, a common trigger for hypos.
glossary.reduced consciousness: Lowered alertness, from drowsy to unrousable, measured by the GCS.
